key_idea: Sample a bounded auxiliary polynomial F on disjoint blocks along quadratic-curvature curves on a torus. By stationary phase, each Fourier mode then lights up only one packed frequency interval, so at most one mode contributes at any angle (the intervals are packed using the Pippenger–Spencer theorem). Defect-sensitive Lovett–Meka partial coloring then rounds the result to signs.
reason: The core mechanism is a striking and reusable idea: chirp-sampling a bounded torus function turns its Fourier modes into disjoint spectral intervals, which caps the sup norm while orthogonality keeps the L2 mass. That idea makes flatness feel natural. It sits inside a fairly heavy architecture (a hypergraph packing via Pippenger–Spencer, coefficient spreading in extra variables, Poisson summation and stationary-phase error bounds, and dyadic discrepancy rounding), so the proof is clearly elegant at its core but carries substantial necessary technical bookkeeping.
recognized: Resembles the Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba flat Littlewood polynomials approach (Rudin–Shapiro-type construction plus Spencer-style rounding), but this all-length limit m_N→1 proof via packing and stationary phase is not one I recognise
